tagline: A tale of exile, court intrigue, and reversal in which a Jewish queen and her cousin save their people from annihilation in the Persian Empire, and God is never named.
overview:
Esther is set in the Persian royal city of Susa during the reign of Xerxes, the king the Hebrew text calls Ahasuerus. It tells how a young Jewish orphan named Hadassah, known by her Persian name Esther, becomes queen after the king deposes his first wife, Vashti; how her cousin and guardian Mordecai refuses to bow to the king's new favorite, Haman; how Haman, in revenge, obtains a royal decree to wipe out every Jew in the empire on a single day chosen by lot; and how Esther, at the risk of her life, goes to the king unsummoned and turns the plot back on the man who made it. Haman dies on the gallows he built for Mordecai, the Jews are given the right to defend themselves, and the day marked for their destruction becomes a day of rescue.

The book ends by explaining the Jewish festival of Purim, named for the pur, the lot Haman cast. Purim is still kept every year, and at it the whole scroll of Esther is read aloud. In Jewish tradition Esther is one of the five Megillot, the festival scrolls, and it is often simply called the Megillah, the scroll.

The most striking thing about Esther is what it leaves out. In the Hebrew text God is never mentioned. No one prays by name, no prophet speaks, no miracle happens, and the covenant, the law, the temple, and Jerusalem are barely in view. Yet the story is full of timing too exact to be chance: a sleepless night, a record read at the right page, a queen in the right place. The book asks its readers, many of whom also lived as a minority under foreign power, to see the hand of a God who is hidden but not absent.
author: The book does not name its author. The Babylonian Talmud assigns its writing to the men of the Great Assembly, the body of leaders that Jewish tradition places in the Persian period after the return from exile. Some older Christian and Jewish writers suggested Mordecai himself, since Esther 9:20 says he recorded these events, but that verse refers to his letters establishing Purim rather than to the book. Modern scholars generally regard the author as an unknown Jewish writer, most likely living in the eastern Diaspora (the scattered Jewish communities outside the land of Israel), who knew Persian court life, vocabulary, and administration well.
date: The story is set in the reign of Xerxes I, who ruled Persia from about 486 to 465 BC. The book itself must have been written after his reign, since it looks back on his days (1:1). Many scholars date its composition to the late Persian period, around the fourth century BC, because its Hebrew belongs to the later stages of the language, it uses a number of Persian loanwords, and it shows no sign of the Greek culture that spread through the region after Alexander the Great's conquests in the 330s BC. Others place it in the early Hellenistic period, in the third or second century BC. A Greek version with substantial additions was circulating by the first century BC.
setting:
The Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great, stretched from India in the east to Egypt, Cush (the upper Nile region), and western Asia Minor in the west. Cyrus had allowed exiled Jews to return to Judah in 539/538 BC, but many stayed where they had settled in Babylonia and Persia. Esther concerns those who stayed. Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran, was one of the empire's royal capitals, and French excavations there uncovered the great palace complex begun by Darius I and used by Xerxes.

Xerxes is well known from the Greek historian Herodotus, who describes his invasion of Greece in 480 BC and its failure at Salamis and Plataea. The feast of Esther 1 falls in Xerxes' third year, before that campaign, and Esther comes to the king in his seventh year, after it. The book's picture of the court fits what is known of Persian government: satraps and governors over provinces, a royal courier system, edicts sent in every local script and language, a king kept at a distance by eunuchs and protocol, and advisers who ranked by their access to him. In chronological terms the events fall between Ezra 6 (the temple's completion in 515 BC) and Ezra 7 (Ezra's return, traditionally dated to about 458 BC).
purpose: The book's stated purpose is to explain and establish Purim, so that the memory of the deliverance would not fade from Jewish descendants (9:28). Beneath that, it served Jews living scattered through a foreign empire. It showed that a Jew could serve faithfully at a pagan court without ceasing to belong to God's people, that hatred of the Jews could arise suddenly and be written into law, and that their survival did not depend on having a king, a temple, or even visible signs of God's presence. For readers who had no prophet and saw no miracles, it taught them to look for God's care in the ordinary turns of history.
story: Esther belongs to the period after the exile, alongside Ezra and Nehemiah. Those books follow the Jews who went back to rebuild Jerusalem; Esther follows those who remained in the east. Its conflict reaches back to much older chapters of Israel's story. Mordecai is introduced as a Benjaminite descended from a man named Kish, a name that recalls the family of King Saul, and Haman is an Agagite, which recalls Agag the Amalekite king whom Saul spared against God's command in 1 Samuel 15. The Amalekites had attacked Israel on the road out of Egypt (Exodus 17), and God had promised war against them from generation to generation. Esther's story replays that old enmity, and this time the descendant of Kish does not fail. The book also stands behind the whole later history of the Jewish people: had Haman's plan succeeded, there would have been no people from whom the promised Messiah could come.
christ: Esther contains no direct prophecy of the Messiah, and it is best to say plainly that its links to Christ are patterns rather than predictions. The largest pattern is the preservation of the people through whom God had promised to bless all nations (Genesis 12:3). The book is one chapter in a long story of threats to Abraham's line and God's quiet keeping of it, a story the New Testament sees completed when Jesus is born a Jew under another empire. Christians have also noticed the shape of Esther's act: one person, placed at the center of power, risks death by going in to the king on behalf of a people condemned by a law they cannot undo, and they are saved. Esther is not a picture of Christ in any detailed sense, and she can only plead, while Christ gives himself. But the story's great reversal, in which the day set for death becomes a day of joy, is the shape the Gospels give to the cross and the empty tomb.
reading:
Esther is a carefully crafted narrative, and much of its meaning comes through its craft. Watch for banquets (the book is full of them, and the plot turns at them), for the irony of characters who get the opposite of what they intend, and for reversals, which the book itself names in 9:1 when the enemies' plan is overturned. The silence about God is deliberate, and a reader should notice where the story seems to hold its breath for him: Mordecai's word that relief may come from another place (4:14), Esther's three-day fast (4:16), the king's sleepless night (6:1).

The book has been read in different ways. Many readers take it as a historical account from the Persian court; others see it as a historical novella built around real institutions and possibly real events, written to explain a festival. Both groups agree that its purpose is theological as well as historical. Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. One is to treat Esther and Mordecai as flawless models; the text presents them with concealment, compromise, and ambition as well as courage. The other is to read the fighting in chapter 9 as a license for revenge; the book stresses that the Jews acted under a royal edict to defend themselves and did not touch the plunder. Readers of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles will also find six longer Greek additions, including prayers of Mordecai and Esther that name God; Protestant and Jewish Bibles follow the shorter Hebrew text.

structure.title: A new queen in Susa
structure.summary: Xerxes deposes Vashti after she refuses his summons, and Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by Mordecai, is chosen as queen without revealing her people. Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king, and his deed is recorded.

structure.title: Haman's decree and Mordecai's challenge
structure.summary: Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman, who obtains a decree to destroy all the Jews on a day chosen by lot. Mordecai urges Esther to go to the king, and she resolves to go, fasting and at the risk of her life.

structure.title: Banquets and the great reversal
structure.summary: Esther invites the king and Haman to two banquets. On the night between them the king cannot sleep, Mordecai is honored by Haman himself, and at the second banquet Esther exposes Haman, who is hanged on his own gallows.

structure.title: A counter-decree and the feast of Purim
structure.summary: Mordecai is given Haman's authority and issues a decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves. On the appointed day they prevail over their enemies, and Mordecai and Esther establish Purim as a yearly festival.

structure.title: The greatness of Mordecai
structure.summary: A brief epilogue records Mordecai's high rank under Xerxes and his work for the good of his people.

themes.title: Hidden providence
themes.body: God is not named, yet the story is built from coincidences that no one arranges: Esther's rise before the danger appears, Mordecai overhearing a plot, a king who cannot sleep on the one night it matters, a record opened to the right place. The book invites readers to see these as the work of a God who governs history without always showing himself. For people living far from the temple and without prophets, this was a way of believing that God had not stopped caring for them.

themes.title: Reversal
themes.body: The book's plot is a series of turnings upside down. Haman plans honor for himself and has to give it to Mordecai; he builds a gallows for Mordecai and dies on it; a decree of destruction is answered by a decree of defense; mourning becomes feasting. The narrator names the pattern when he says the enemies' plan was overturned (9:1). The reversals teach that the powers who seem to control history do not have the last word.

themes.title: Identity under pressure
themes.body: Esther begins by hiding who she is and ends by naming her people before the king at the risk of her life. Mordecai, by contrast, will not bow to Haman and openly says he is a Jew. The book explores what it costs to belong to God's people in a culture that rewards blending in, and it treats the moment when concealment has to end as the moment of true courage.

themes.title: Law, power, and the vulnerable
themes.body: Persian law in Esther cannot be revoked, and it is used by powerful men to settle personal grievances: a queen deposed for refusing to be displayed, an entire people condemned because one man would not bow. The book shows how easily law can be turned into an instrument of pride and hatred, and how those with some access to power are responsible for those who have none.

themes.title: Remembering deliverance
themes.body: The book closes by turning a rescue into a festival, with feasting, gifts to one another, and gifts to the poor. Remembering is itself an act of faith: each Purim retells the story so that later generations, facing their own Hamans, would know they had been preserved before.

keyChapters.why: Esther becomes queen while hiding her identity, and Mordecai's unrewarded rescue of the king is recorded, setting up everything that follows.
Haman's decree to destroy the Jews reveals the depth of the threat and ties the story to the ancient conflict between Israel and Amalek.
Mordecai's challenge that Esther may have come to the kingdom “for such a time as this” and her decision to go to the king form the turning point of the book.
The king's sleepless night and Haman's humiliation are the book's clearest picture of hidden providence at work.
Esther names her people and her enemy, and Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
The day of destruction becomes a day of deliverance, and the feast of Purim is established.

parts.body:
Esther is the seventeenth book of the Bible. It has ten chapters, and it tells how a young Jewish woman became queen of Persia and, with her cousin Mordecai, saved her people from a plan to destroy them all on a single day.

The story is set in Susa, a royal city of the Persian empire, in the reign of Xerxes, whom the Hebrew text calls Ahasuerus. The king deposes his queen, Vashti, and Esther, an orphan raised by Mordecai, is taken into the palace and made queen without revealing that she is a Jew. Mordecai will not bow to the king's favorite, Haman, and Haman, in revenge, obtains a decree to wipe out every Jew in the empire on a day chosen by lot. Esther goes to the king uncalled, at the risk of her life, and the plot turns back on the man who made it. The day set for the Jews' destruction becomes a day of rescue.

The book ends by explaining the feast of Purim, named for the pur, the lot Haman cast. Jews still keep it every year, and at it the whole scroll of Esther is read aloud.

The most striking thing about the book is what it leaves out. In the Hebrew text God is never named. No one prays by name, no prophet speaks and no miracle happens. Yet the story is full of timing too exact to be chance: a queen in the right place, a sleepless night, a record read at the right page. Mordecai's question to Esther is as close as the book comes to saying it: ‘And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?’ (4:14).

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Esther belongs to the years after the exile, beside Ezra and Nehemiah. Those books follow the Jews who went back to rebuild Jerusalem. Esther follows those who stayed in the east. Cyrus had let the exiles go home in 539 or 538 BC, but many had settled in Babylonia and Persia, and the book assumes Jews scattered through the provinces of the empire. In time, its events fall between Ezra 6, the temple finished in 515 BC, and Ezra 7, Ezra's return in about 458 BC.

In the Hebrew Bible, Esther stands among the Writings, as one of the five short scrolls read at the festivals, the Megillot. It is often simply called the Megillah, the scroll. Christian Bibles place it last among the books of history, after Nehemiah.

Its conflict reaches back to much older chapters. Mordecai is introduced as a Benjaminite descended from a man named Kish (2:5), a name that recalls the family of King Saul. Haman is an Agagite (3:1), which most readers connect with Agag, the Amalekite king whom Saul spared against God's command (1 Samuel 15). The book does not say so outright, but many readers hear in it the old enmity between Israel and Amalek played out again.

The book does not name its author. The Babylonian Talmud assigns its writing to the men of the Great Assembly, the body of leaders that Jewish tradition places in the Persian period. Some older Jewish and Christian writers suggested Mordecai himself, since 9:20 says that he recorded these events, but that verse refers to his letters about Purim rather than to the book. Most modern scholars think of an unknown Jewish writer, probably living in the scattered communities of the east, who knew Persian court life, its words and its government well.

The book was written after the reign of Xerxes, since it looks back on ‘the days of Xerxes’ (1:1). Many scholars date it to the late Persian period, around the fourth century BC, because its Hebrew belongs to the later stages of the language, it uses many Persian words, and it shows no sign of the Greek culture that spread through the region after Alexander's conquests. Others place it in the early Greek period, in the third or second century BC.

The text has a history too. A Greek version with six long additions was circulating by the first century BC. The additions include prayers of Mordecai and Esther that name God, and they stand in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Protestant and Jewish Bibles follow the shorter Hebrew text.

Christians who receive Esther as God's word hold more than one of these views, and these notes take no side among them.

The book fits the Persian court well. It knows the name and extent of Xerxes' empire, the palace at Susa, the royal couriers, the decrees sent in every script and language, and a great many Persian words. French excavations at Susa uncovered the great palace complex begun by Darius I and used by Xerxes, with its columned audience hall.

But the Greek historian Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther, and no record outside the Bible names a queen called Vashti or Esther, or a chief minister called Haman. A clay tablet from about the time of Xerxes mentions an official named Marduka serving at Susa, and the name appears in other Persian records, but whether any of these refers to the Mordecai of this book cannot be shown.

Readers answer in several ways. Some identify Vashti with Amestris, noting that the names could be related and that Herodotus may not record every change at court, so that Esther would be a later wife who held the title of queen. Others note that Persian kings had several wives, and that the Greek sources are incomplete and often hostile. Still others read Esther as a historical novella: a story set in a real court, built around real institutions and possibly a real rescue, but told with a storyteller's freedom to explain the feast of Purim.

Readers who differ on this question can still agree on what the book teaches. These notes set out what is known and take no side.

Xerxes I reigned over Persia from about 486 to 465 BC. The feast of chapter 1 falls in his third year (1:3), about 483 BC. In the years that followed he invaded Greece, and Greek sources tell of his defeat at Salamis in 480 BC and at Plataea in 479 BC, though the book says nothing of these wars.

Esther comes to the king in the tenth month of his seventh year (2:16), about 479 or 478 BC. Haman casts the lot in the first month of the twelfth year (3:7), about 474 BC, and it falls on the twelfth month, nearly a year away. Mordecai's counter-decree is written two months later (8:9), and the day itself, the thirteenth of Adar, comes in about 473 BC. Xerxes was later killed in a palace plot in 465 BC.

The dates are approximate, and they depend on reading the book's years as Xerxes' own. Those who read the book as a novella take the dates as part of its setting rather than as a record.

Esther is a carefully crafted story, and much of its meaning comes through its craft.

Watch for banquets. The book is full of them, and the plot turns at them: the king's feasts in chapter 1, a banquet for the new queen in chapter 2, the king and Haman drinking while the city is in confusion in chapter 3, Esther's two banquets in chapters 5 and 7, and the feasting of Purim. The word for feast, mishteh, comes from the verb to drink, and it appears more often in Esther than in any other book.

Watch for law. A Persian word for law or decree, dat, appears about twenty times. Persian law in Esther cannot be revoked, and powerful men use it to settle personal grievances.

Above all, watch for reversals. Characters get the opposite of what they intend. Haman plans honor for himself and has to give it to Mordecai. He builds a gallows for Mordecai and dies on it. A decree of destruction is answered by a decree of defense, and mourning becomes feasting. The book names the pattern itself: ‘their plan was overturned’ (9:1). Many scholars see the whole book arranged around chapter 6, the king's sleepless night, with the events before it mirrored by the events after it.

And notice what is told and what is kept hidden. Esther hides her people at first; Mordecai tells of a plot; Esther at last names her people and her enemy before the king. When to keep silent and when to speak drives the plot.

parts.h: The God who is never named
parts.body:
Esther is one of only two books of the Hebrew Bible that never mention God, with the Song of Songs. Its silence is most striking at the book's turning point, where Mordecai speaks of relief ‘from another place’ (4:14) and Esther calls a fast without a word about prayer.

Readers have explained the silence in several ways. Many see it as deliberate: the book shows God working hiddenly, through ordinary choices and apparent coincidences, as he often seems to work in a world where he is not seen. Some suggest that a book meant to be read at a noisy festival, or written for Jews living under a foreign empire, spoke of God with reserve. Some take another place as a reverent way of pointing to God without naming him; others read it as meaning only another human source of help.

Ancient readers felt the silence too. The Greek translation adds long prayers by Mordecai and Esther that name God often. Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible not found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and rabbis into the second century AD are recorded debating its place among the holy books. Yet it stayed in the canon of both synagogue and church.

What the Hebrew text does is leave the reader to see the hand that the characters do not name. A fast that a first reader would take to mean prayer. A sleepless king. A record read at the right page. The book does not draw the lesson for the reader. It trusts the reader to notice.

parts.h: A queen who refused, and a girl who was taken
parts.body:
The book opens with power on display. Xerxes, who ‘reigned over 127 provinces from India to Cush’ (1:1), shows off his wealth for 180 days and then holds a week-long feast in Susa. On the last day, drunk, he orders Queen Vashti to be brought before his guests ‘wearing her royal crown, to display her beauty to the people and officials’ (1:11). She refuses. The king is furious, and on his counselors' advice he deposes her by a decree that cannot be repealed, and sends letters to every province proclaiming ‘that every man should be master of his own household’ (1:22). The chapter is close to satire: the most powerful man in the world cannot command his own wife, and answers one woman's refusal with a law for the whole empire.

The text does not explain Vashti's reasons. Interpreters have seen her as defiant, or as rightly refusing to be put on show and degraded. Either way, her refusal costs her the crown.

To replace her, the king's servants gather young women from every province into the royal harem. ‘Esther was also taken to the palace’ (2:8). The book tells this plainly and without romance. A young woman taken into the harem did not choose to go and could not choose to leave. After a year of beauty treatments she went in to the king for one night, and then to the house of the concubines, where she might never see him again unless he called her by name. Esther, an orphan from a scattered and powerless people, was one of many young women whose lives were shaped by a king's whim. She is chosen and crowned queen, and on Mordecai's instruction she does not reveal her people.

The Bible does not hide the coercion of women in this story, and these notes do not either. It shows God working through, not only around, a situation that was not right.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: A decree to destroy a people
parts.body:
The king promotes Haman the Agagite above all his officials and orders everyone to bow to him. Mordecai will not. When asked why, he says only that he is a Jew. Haman is filled with rage, and when he learns who Mordecai's people are, ‘he scorned the notion of laying hands on Mordecai alone’ (3:6). He resolves to destroy them all.

A lot is cast to choose the day, and it falls nearly a year away. Then Haman goes to the king with a speech that is a masterpiece of manipulation. He never names the Jews. “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples of every province of your kingdom. Their laws are different from everyone else’s, and they do not obey the king’s laws” (3:8). He mixes a half-truth with a lie, appeals to the king's interests, and offers to pay ten thousand talents of silver into the treasury. The king does not even ask which people he is condemning. Letters go out to every province with the king's seal, ordering the destruction of all the Jews, young and old, on the thirteenth of Adar.

The chapter's last line sets two scenes side by side: ‘Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion’ (3:15).

This is one of the clearest pictures in the Bible of how hatred of the Jewish people can arise suddenly and be written into law. A personal grudge becomes a plan to destroy a whole people in a single verse. The book holds that hatred up to be seen for what it is. Nothing in it is ever a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people, or any people.

parts.h: For such a time as this
parts.body:
When the decree is published, Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and goes through the city wailing. In every province there is great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping and lamenting.

Esther, in the palace, learns of it through a servant, and Mordecai urges her to go to the king and plead for her people. She explains the danger: anyone who goes to the king in the inner court uncalled is put to death, unless the king holds out his gold scepter, and she has not been called for thirty days. Mordecai's answer is the heart of the book: “For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (4:14).

Esther decides. She asks all the Jews in Susa to fast for her for three days, night and day, and she and her maids will fast too. “After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” (4:16).

Up to here Esther has been taken and moved by others. Now she gives the orders, and Mordecai goes and does all that she commanded. The moment when concealment has to end is the moment of true courage.

parts.h: Banquets, a sleepless night, and a gallows
parts.body:
On the third day Esther puts on her royal robes and stands in the inner court. The king sees her, ‘she found favor in his sight’ (5:2), and he holds out the scepter. He offers her up to half the kingdom. She asks only that the king and Haman come to a banquet, and at the banquet she asks them to come to another the next day. Haman goes home delighted, sees Mordecai at the gate refusing to rise, and on his wife's advice he builds a gallows for Mordecai.

‘That night sleep escaped the king’ (6:1). He has the royal records read to him and learns that Mordecai once saved his life and was never rewarded. At that moment Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's death. The king asks him, “What should be done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor?” (6:6). Haman, sure that he is the man, describes a royal robe, a royal horse and a public parade, and he is ordered to do it all for Mordecai.

At the second banquet, Esther finally speaks. She asks for her own life and her people's, for ‘my people and I have been sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation’ (7:4). The king demands to know who has done this, and she names him: “The adversary and enemy is this wicked man” (7:6), Haman. ‘So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai’ (7:10).

Nothing in these chapters is a miracle, and yet everything arrives exactly on time.

parts.h: The day overturned, and the feast of Purim
parts.body:
Haman is dead, but his decree still stands. A Persian decree sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked. Esther weeps at the king's feet, and the king lets Mordecai write a second decree in his name, allowing the Jews in every city to gather and defend themselves on the thirteenth of Adar against anyone who would attack them. The new decree repeats the wording of Haman's almost word for word. Every instrument once used against the Jews is now used for them.

On the appointed day, ‘the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, but their plan was overturned’ (9:1). The Jews fight those who sought to harm them, in Susa and in the provinces. The book gives large numbers of the dead, and three times it says that the Jews did not lay a hand on the plunder. At Esther's request, the fighting in Susa continues a second day.

This is the hardest part of the book for many readers, and it should be read as such. Readers weigh it in different ways. The Jews act under a royal decree permitting defense on a day set for their destruction, and they strike those who hated them, not neutral neighbors. Their refusal of plunder suggests that they fought to survive and not for gain. Esther's request for a second day is harder to explain; some see it as ending a continuing threat in the capital, and others as going too far. Some scholars read the numbers as part of a stylized story; others defend the book's history, noting that the ancient versions already give different figures. Faithful readers differ on how far the narrator approves. The book records these events without lingering on them, and it does not hold them up as a pattern.

Nothing in Esther gives anyone today a warrant to harm anyone, or to take revenge on any people. The New Testament forbids personal vengeance (Romans 12:19).

The book ends with a feast. Mordecai and Esther write letters establishing Purim: days ‘of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor’ (9:22). Purim was not one of the feasts commanded in the law of Moses. The community itself established it, and it is kept to this day, on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, with the scroll read aloud and the congregation drowning out Haman's name.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Esther
parts.body:
The New Testament never quotes Esther, and it is wise to say so plainly.

A few scenes echo it. When Herod Antipas promises a dancer, “up to half my kingdom” (Mark 6:23), he speaks the same royal formula that the Persian king spoke to Esther (5:3). And the feasting and gift-giving of Purim stand behind a line in Revelation about people who ‘will celebrate and send one another gifts’ (Revelation 11:10).

Some Christians have read Esther, who risked her life before a king to plead for a condemned people, as a picture of Christ. The book's own introduction calls its links to Christ patterns rather than predictions, and says that Esther is not a picture of Christ in any detailed sense. The New Testament does not draw that line, and these notes do not draw it either.

What the book does give is a picture of a people kept alive under a foreign empire, in a story where God is hidden and not absent. Nothing in Esther, or in how Christians read it, is a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people. The book was written to help them remember that they had been kept safe before.

A few habits will help a new reader.

Read it in one sitting, as a story. It is meant to be heard whole, as it is at Purim.

Watch for the banquets, the reversals and the silence about God. Notice where the story seems to hold its breath: Mordecai's word about another place (4:14), Esther's three-day fast (4:16), the king's sleepless night (6:1).

Do not make Esther and Mordecai flawless models. The book shows them with concealment and compromise as well as courage, and it does not moralize. Do not make Vashti a villain either. And read the fighting in chapter 9 with care, as a book's record of a people's survival and not as a license for revenge.

Read Esther beside Ezra and Nehemiah. Together they show God's people after the exile, some rebuilding Jerusalem and some living as a minority far from it, both kept by the same God.

hard.line: Is Esther history? Greek sources name Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther.
Vashti refuses to be put on show before drunken guests, and loses her crown: defiance, or a right refusal?
Young women taken into the king's harem without their consent, and Esther among them.
Esther hides her people at Mordecai's command: prudence, or compromise?
Mordecai's family was carried into exile in 597 BC, more than a century before: whom does the verse mean?
Why Mordecai would not bow to Haman, when Israelites bowed to kings and officials elsewhere.
A decree to destroy a whole people on one day, and how the book holds that hatred up to be seen.
The book's turning point names neither God nor prayer: relief ‘from another place’.
‘And if I perish, I perish’: Esther goes to the king against the law.
A gallows fifty cubits high, and what the word for it means.
A sleepless king and a record read at the right page: providence, or coincidence?
Esther is silent as Haman begs for his life: is she cruel?
Does Mordecai's decree permit the killing of women and children? The Hebrew can be read two ways.

Purim, a feast the law of Moses did not command, kept to this day.

words.line: From pur, an Akkadian word for the lot Haman cast to choose the day (3:7). The feast named after it celebrates the day turned to rescue (9:26).
The Hebrew dat, a Persian word for law or decree, used about twenty times. A Persian decree could not be repealed (1:19; 8:8).
The Hebrew mishteh, from the verb to drink. The plot moves from feast to feast, from the king's banquets to the feasting of Purim (1:3; 9:22).
The Hebrew chen: the goodwill of a superior. Esther finds favor with everyone who sees her (2:15), and with the king at the moment her life is at stake (5:2).
Haman's family name (3:1). Most readers connect it with Agag, the Amalekite king of 1 Samuel 15.
The Hebrew shamad, to wipe out. It names Haman's purpose (3:6) and the words of his decree (3:13).
The Hebrew hatstsalah, a word found only in 4:14. Mordecai is sure deliverance will come; the question is whether Esther will be part of it.
The Hebrew et, a fitting or appointed moment. Esther may have come to the kingdom for such a time as this (4:14).
The Hebrew tsum. Esther asks the Jews of Susa to fast for three days (4:16); in the Old Testament fasting goes with prayer.
The Hebrew yeqar, honor or esteem, used more in Esther than anywhere else. The man whom the king delights to honor turns out to be Mordecai (6:6).
The Hebrew haphakh, to turn over. The enemies' plan was overturned (9:1), and sorrow was turned to joy (9:22). It is the key word of the book.
The Hebrew mishneh. Mordecai ends the book second only to the king (10:3).
The Hebrew shalom: wholeness and well-being. Mordecai spoke peace to all his people (10:3).
Esther's Hebrew name, meaning myrtle (2:7). Esther is her Persian name.
The scroll: the Jewish name for the book of Esther, one of the five scrolls read at the festivals, read aloud whole at Purim.

timeline.what: Cyrus lets the exiles go home. Many stay in Babylonia and Persia (Ezra 1).
The second temple is finished in Jerusalem (Ezra 6:15).
Xerxes I, the Ahasuerus of the book, reigns over Persia.
The king's feast in his third year, and Vashti's refusal (1:3, 12).
Xerxes' invasion of Greece ends in defeat at Salamis and Plataea. The book does not mention it.
Esther is taken to the king in the tenth month of his seventh year and made queen (2:16-17).
In the first month of the twelfth year, the lot is cast and Haman's decree goes out (3:7, 12).
Mordecai's decree lets the Jews defend themselves (8:9).
The thirteenth of Adar: the day of destruction is overturned (9:1).
Xerxes is killed in a plot at his own court.
Ezra goes to Jerusalem, on the traditional dating (Ezra 7).

timeline.when: The fourth century BC, or later
timeline.what: The book is written, in the late Persian period on many views, or in the third or second century BC on others.
Second Maccabees calls the fourteenth of Adar Mordecai's day: Purim is known in Judea.
A Greek version of Esther with six long additions, including prayers that name God, is in circulation.
Rabbis are recorded still debating Esther's place among the holy books.
Athanasius lists Esther among the books to be read.

places.line: Mordecai's family was carried into exile from here with King Jeconiah (2:6). The whole story of Esther takes place far to the east, in Susa.
